title: Find and Fix Typos with Vim’s Spell Checker
summary: Chapter 20 covers Vim's built-in spell checker across four tips. Tip 120 shows how to enable it with :set spell and operate it from Normal mode using ]s, [s, z=, and the zg/zw/zug family. Tip 121 explains the buffer-local 'spelllang' option, regional English variants such as en_us, and how Vim offers to download missing spell files via spellfile.vim, while Tip 122 shows how zg/zw additions persist in a spell file and how the 'spellfile' option can point at a separate jargon word list. Tip 123 demonstrates fixing misspellings without leaving Insert mode using the <C-x>s spelling autocompletion.

commands.meaning: Enable Vim's built-in spell checker so unrecognized words are flagged
Jump to the next spelling error
Jump to the previous spelling error
Ask Vim for a list of suggested corrections for the word under the cursor
Add the word under the cursor to a spell file
Mark the word under the cursor as misspelled, removing it from the spell file
Revert the zg or zw command for the word under the cursor
In the z= suggestion list, accept the first suggestion and replace the word
commands.evidence: We can replace the misspelled word with “Your” by pressing 1<CR>. If the list doesn’t contain what we’re looking for, we can dismiss it by pressing <Esc>.

commands.meaning: Prefix z= with a count to apply the numbered suggestion directly, without the prompt
commands.evidence: We can skip the prompt altogether by prefixing the z= command with a count, which instructs Vim to use the numbered suggestion. If we’re confident that the first suggestion will be correct, we can run 1z= to fix it in one go.

commands.meaning: Restrict accepted spellings to American English
Switch the buffer to the French spell file, prompting a download if it is missing
With a count, add the word to the numbered spell file (here the jargon list); 1zg targets the default list
commands.evidence: For each word that the spell checker flags incorrectly, I now have a choice. I could press 2zg to add it to my list of Vim terminology, or 1zg to add it to the default word list.

commands.meaning: Switch back to Insert mode at the end of the line after fixing a typo in Normal mode
commands.evidence: To fix the mistake, we could switch to Normal mode, use the [s command to jump back to the spelling mistake, and then use 1z= to fix it. Having made the correction, we could then switch back to Insert mode with the A command, continuing where we left off.

concepts.name: SpellBad syntax highlighting marks flagged words
concepts.evidence: The word “Yoru” should now be flagged with the SpellBad syntax highlighting. Typically, that means the word will be underlined with a red dashed line, but how it looks will depend on which color scheme you use.

concepts.name: Separating composition from a final spell-checking pass
concepts.evidence: When writing, I prefer to separate the composition and spell-checking processes into separate tasks. I’ll often disable the spell checker while I write to avoid being nagged each time I make a mistake. Then I’ll make a final pass through the document with the spell checker enabled, fixing the typos it flags.

concepts.name: Buffer-local 'spelllang' option
concepts.evidence: When we enable Vim’s spell checker, it compares words against an English dictionary by default. We can change this by tweaking the ‘spelllang’ option (see 'spelllang'ⓘ). This isn’t a global setting; ‘spelllang’ is always local to the buffer. That means it’s possible to work simultaneously on two or more documents and use a different spell file for each—handy if you’re bilingual.

concepts.name: Regional English spelling variants
concepts.evidence: With this setting, “moustache” would be flagged as a misspelling, but “mustache” would be permitted. Other supported regions include en_au, en_ca, en_gb, and en_nz. See spell-remarksⓘ for more details.

concepts.name: Words added with zg persist across sessions in a spell file
concepts.evidence: Vim records words added to the dictionary in a spell file so that they persist from one session to another. The name of the spell file is derived from the language and file encoding.

concepts.name: 'spellfile' option can hold multiple word lists
concepts.evidence: With the ‘spellfile’ option, we can specify the path of the file where Vim tracks words added or removed using the zg and zw commands (see 'spellfile'ⓘ). Vim allows us to specify more than one spell file simultaneously, which means we can maintain multiple word lists.

concepts.name: Separate spell file for specialist jargon
concepts.evidence: This book contains many strings of text that don’t count as words in English, including Vim commands (such as ciw) and settings (such as ‘spelllang’). I don’t want Vim to keep flagging these as misspelled, but neither do I want to tell Vim to consider them as valid English words. As a compromise, I maintain a separate word list of Vim terminology. I can load this as a spell file any time that I’m writing about Vim.

concepts.name: Count prefix selects which spell file zg writes to
concepts.evidence: For each word that the spell checker flags incorrectly, I now have a choice. I could press 2zg to add it to my list of Vim terminology, or 1zg to add it to the default word list.

concepts.name: Spelling autocompletion without leaving Insert mode
concepts.evidence: Vim’s spelling autocompletion allows us to fix typos without even having to leave Insert mode.

concepts.name: <C-x>s scans backward to the nearest misspelled word
concepts.evidence: When we trigger an autocomplete command, Vim usually offers suggestions on how to complete the word at the current cursor position. But in the case of <C-x>s, Vim scans backward from the cursor position, stopping when it finds a misspelled word. It then builds a word list from suggested corrections and presents them in an autocomplete pop-up menu. We can choose a result using any of the techniques described in Tip 113.

concepts.name: Normal-mode repair sequence: [s, then 1z=, then A
concepts.evidence: To fix the mistake, we could switch to Normal mode, use the [s command to jump back to the spelling mistake, and then use 1z= to fix it. Having made the correction, we could then switch back to Insert mode with the A command, continuing where we left off.

problems.evidence: Vim usually ships with a spell file for the English language only, but it’s easy to install others. Also, as we’ll see in Tip 121, we can switch between American and British English (beside others). And if a word is incorrectly marked as misspelled, adding it to a spell file is a simple matter, as we’ll see in Tip 122.
problems.note: Reads '(beside others)'; the idiomatic form is 'besides others' (or 'among others'), so this is either a source typo or a dropped character.
